articles.title: Trump speaks with Netanyahu shortly after discussing military operations with senior commanders
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, as the United States prepares to resume strikes on Iran, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal.
The call took place after Trump discussed options for resuming military operations with senior military commanders.
Israel's defense establishment has remained ambiguous regarding preparations for a possible escalation with Iran, as the White House attempted to offer the Iranian regime another opportunity to return to negotiations, according to Israeli defense assessments.
Defense officials assess that the Iranians, who are facing an economic crisis that is worsening from week to week, will not sign an agreement requiring them to completely abandon their nuclear program, and certainly will not agree to stop producing ballistic missiles that now also threaten Europe.
Accordingly, the assessment is that Iran is merely attempting to buy time. Iran has reportedly been deliberately prolonging negotiations ahead of the US midterm elections.
US, Israel posture for strikes, but war unlikely to occur before midterm elections
Defense officials further assess that despite preparations by the US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) for a possible strike on Iran, the White House will not order an operation against the Iranian regime before the US midterm elections unless it detects preparations for a surprise attack.
The US and Israel have also reportedly drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms.
It is worth noting that more than 3,000 American troops are currently stationed in Israel, and no sharp increase was recorded in the number of US military aircraft redirected to the country during the previous week. This contrasts with the unprecedented deployment of US military refueling aircraft that filled the runways at Ben-Gurion Airport and Ramon Airport, alongside a significant presence at Israeli Air Force bases.
US Air Force aircrafts arrive at IAF bases
Last week, ten US Air Force (USAF) transport aircraft arrived at IAF bases in southern Israel as part of a larger Middle East air convoy transferring military equipment across the region, KAN News reported.
The aircraft, which came from Texas' Fort Bliss base, are likely stocked with air defense systems intended to protect regional assets amid reported US warnings earlier this week of a potential "short, focused war with Iran," according to KAN.
Other aircraft in the air convoy landed in Jordan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, with the KAN report coming after an earlier report that the US had transferred an additional Patriot system to the region pending a potential escalation with Iran.
An Israeli source told KAN that the US and Israel are closely coordinating on Iran, with reports that an additional US naval aircraft carrier will join American forces in the region, alongside an additional Marine unit.\
Two weeks ago, dozens of Israel Air Force fighter jets flew "as far as the Iranian border" before turning around and returning to Israel in a practice sortie, according to an Axios report citing US and Israeli officials.

articles.title: Israel completes 'preparations' for Iran confrontation as US weighs options — report
articles.body:
Israel has completed preparations for a renewed military attack on Iran, whilst US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper has presented President Donald Trump with military options for resuming attacks, the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported.
“The Israeli military has finalised defensive and offensive readiness for a potential return to combat, though any decision to launch an offensive remains with Trump as diplomatic contacts continue.”
Citing unnamed political sources, the daily reported that Israel is approaching another round of fighting, but its leadership cannot unilaterally initiate the campaign, which hinges on whether Washington pursues an agreement with Tehran or orders coordinated strikes.
Preparations have advanced beyond planning.
The Israeli air force has carried out multiple long-range drills involving dozens of fighter jets and mid-air refuelling tankers across Syrian and Iraqi airspace towards Iranian frontiers to rehearse potential strike corridors.
Strategic dilemmas
Cooper tabled strike plans during a White House briefing attended by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, though no order to resume combat has been given.
In recent days, 10 US military transport aircraft have landed at Israeli airbases delivering equipment, coinciding with broader American force reinforcements.
Sources noted a fundamental strategic dilemma: the lack of clearly defined US operational objectives.
Striking Iranian nuclear facilities, missile infrastructure, and military assets would not guarantee government collapse or policy shifts, though Washington could leverage threats to extract concessionary terms.
Regional escalation remains a critical hazard, with officials warning Hezbollah could enter the fray, stretching Israeli air defences and interceptor stockpiles.
Concurrently, indirect contacts mediated by Qatar continue, exploring prospective terms regarding Iran's nuclear programme, the Strait of Hormuz, and economic incentives, with Russia and China as potential guarantors.
Hostilities originally erupted on February 28, following joint US-Israeli strikes, before an April truce broke down into renewed exchanges in July amid stalled diplomacy.

articles.title: Rubio defends Russian G-20 presence despite criticism from allies
articles.body:
Rubio defends Russian G-20 presence despite criticism from allies
- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended keeping Russia in G-20 talks, saying dialogue is needed to end the war in Ukraine and avoid wider conflict.
- EU and other allies criticised the move, warning it could normalise Russia’s war crimes and reward President Vladimir Putin while the war continues.
- The Atlanta meeting showed deep division, with no “family photo”, tense exchanges with Sergei Lavrov, and calls from some leaders for Russia to admit wrongdoing.
AI generated
ATLANTA - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the US decision to include Russia in this year’s Group of 20 (G-20) meetings after criticism from the European Union and other allies, calling dialogue the only way to end the war in Ukraine.
Rubio spoke on Oct 31 after a two-day meeting in Atlanta where the US scrapped a traditional “family photo” meant to display unity among officials after some refused to take a picture with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
The rejection by the EU, Germany, Poland, Canada and others created a powerful symbolic division between the US – trying to coax Russia to talks – and allies who say they don’t want to reward President Vladimir Putin for his invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago. The war has killed more than one million people and wracked Europe like no conflict since World War II, while also disrupting shipping and raising energy and food prices around the world.
President Donald Trump thought it “important that Russia be a part of the G-20 conversation,” Rubio told reporters in Atlanta. “What he doesn’t accept is the idea that somehow meeting with someone legitimises them or makes you agree with everything that they do. It’s very simple: everybody wants there to be a deal that brings about an end to this war. How can you do a deal unless you’re meeting with them?” he said.
Rubio’s EU counterpart, Kaja Kallas, said that Putin’s potential attendance at the G-20 leaders’ summit in Miami in December would risk regularising Russia’s return to international forums while its war in Ukraine rages.
The US invitation to the Russian leader “poses a lot of big questions”, Kallas said in an interview on Bloomberg This Weekend on Oct 31. It risks “normalising the war crimes being committed every day now” in Ukraine, she added.
Many leaders were unhappy with Trump’s announcement earlier in October that he would waive some tariffs and sanctions on Russia as part of a deal with Putin to let Russia export diesel to overseas markets.
Trump has invited Putin to the Florida G-20 meeting, but the Kremlin has yet to say if he’ll accept. Rubio on Oct 31 floated the possibility that the pair could meet sooner, at the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit in Shenzhen, China. Rubio said that beyond the war in Ukraine, it’s important for the US to talk to Russia given the nation’s nuclear weapons stockpile and the need to avoid conflict.
Including Moscow “gives Russia everything it wants on the world stage, without having to stop its war of aggression or cede anything in Ukraine”, said Torrey Taussig, a former Biden administration official who is now at the Atlantic Council. “It sends the message that the US wants to get back to business as usual with Russia and that the West didn’t have the staying power, which Putin has been banking on throughout the war.”
Lavrov, in comments to reporters in Atlanta, repeated Putin’s suggestion that President Volodymyr Zelensky travel to Moscow to meet him. That’s an idea that the Ukrainian leader has repeatedly rejected, saying it would be inappropriate to visit the aggressor, as well as citing continued attacks on Ukraine and safety and security risks.
Lavrov said that it makes sense for Russia and the US to work together in areas where their interests align, while calling the treatment of Russia by European nations an “arrogant boycott”.
In one session, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov: “If you had the courage to tell the truth and to do what is right, you would tell Putin that he is not winning this war and will not win,” according to a transcript from the British embassy.
Rubio said that he didn’t have formal bilateral talks with Lavrov in Atlanta. Photos posted to social media from a reception that Rubio hosted on Oct 30 night at the Georgia Aquarium showed that Rubio spoke with Lavrov, but that the Russian otherwise largely was alone and kept to himself in the ballroom framed by tanks filled with beluga whales and manta rays.
Video from the plenary sessions showed him speaking with counterparts from Saudi Arabia and Turkey, but not Western European officials. Lavrov also met with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi to discuss issues including a Japanese journalist detained in Russia.
“Russia has isolated itself, and that was visibly present at the reception last night,” Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said in a phone interview on Oct 31. “The decisions that his country has repeatedly taken are completely contrary to international law. They are inhumane, and the failure of Russia, including Vladimir Putin and Sergei Lavrov, to acknowledge wrongdoing and the devastation to human life that they are repeatedly causing is remarkable and reprehensible.”
“The fact that he comes here to trot out tired old Kremlin talking points is beneath the conversation that we have here at the G-20, where countries come together to collaborate to address issues of global concern and conflict,” she said. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Rubio Casts Doubts On Quick Deal To End War In Ukraine, Defends Russian Contacts
articles.body:
ATLANTA, Georgia -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was unsure whether a negotiated end to the war in Ukraine was possible, while European officials told RFE/RL the top US diplomat also privately expressed doubts that Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend December’s Miami G20 summit.
The European officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Rubio also privately shared his doubts with Western counterparts of a peace deal in the coming months during the two days of G20 foreign ministers' talks in Atlanta, which wrapped up on October 31.
Rubio's public remarks at his closing news conference were notably cautious. Asked by RFE/RL whether he believed a negotiated settlement was achievable given Moscow's unchanged position, he said Washington was still trying to establish whether an agreement could be reached.
“I don't know if negotiated peace is achievable in Ukraine. That's what we're trying to find out," Rubio said. "I don't think anyone here is claiming that we're on the verge of a negotiated settlement.”
He said President Donald Trump's envoys, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, were devoting much of their time to the Ukraine and Iran portfolios. "But I'm not here to tell you we're on the verge of one," Rubio said, adding that he hoped an agreement could eventually be reached.
He also clarified that Ukraine negotiations were not discussed at the Atlanta G20 gathering itself.
Putin's Miami Invitation
Rubio was equally careful when asked whether Putin would attend the December summit, which Trump plans to host at his Doral resort in Florida.
"I don't even know if President Putin is going to come to Miami. They haven't announced that and they haven't confirmed that," he said.
The three European officials told RFE/RL that Rubio had privately expressed doubts that the Russian leader would accept the invitation.
They also said the secretary of state defended the administration's decision to invite Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov to Atlanta and extend an invitation to Putin, arguing that diplomatic engagement was necessary to achieve a settlement.
"How can you have a negotiated settlement between Russia and Ukraine if you don't have the ability to talk to both Russia and Ukraine?" Rubio later asked when pressed by reporters.
He said Trump did not regard meeting or talking with a foreign leader as legitimizing that leader's actions or agreeing with everything he stood for.
Rubio also cited Russia's nuclear arsenal as a reason for maintaining communication between Washington and Moscow, regardless of the state of bilateral relations.
"It is always important that the United States and Russia have communications at some level because of the danger of escalation in the future," he said.
Describing his own interaction with Lavrov in Atlanta, Rubio said the two had not held a formal meeting. They spoke briefly about the possibility of their countries' leaders interacting at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering, but made no firm commitments concerning the G20 summit.
The Western officials said Rubio's private assessment also covered Ukraine's potential NATO membership, which he reportedly described as unrealistic in the short term and unacceptable to Putin.
Rubio reportedly warned that Russia's acquisition of the entire Donbas region would not satisfy the Kremlin's territorial ambitions. It "will not end Russian appetite," he told the Europeans, according to the officials.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reported private remarks.
Black Sea Opening
While Rubio offered little public optimism about a comprehensive peace agreement, he identified a more limited diplomatic objective that Washington hopes could produce results: a cease-fire covering the Black Sea.
European officials pressed Moscow during the Atlanta talks to halt attacks affecting shipping in the strategic waterway, which is vital for Ukrainian agricultural exports.
Asked whether international efforts to secure such an arrangement were gaining momentum, Rubio cautioned against overstating the prospects. "I wouldn't call it momentum," he told reporters, describing instead a growing interest among countries in acting as guarantors or facilitators of an agreement.
He said Washington was examining proposals submitted by Turkey and that India had also expressed interest in putting forward ideas. "We'd like to achieve it. It doesn't solve the war, but at least it solves a unique aspect of it," Rubio said.
He warned that disruptions to grain and energy shipments were creating serious consequences for vulnerable countries, particularly those dependent on food imports. "This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well," he said.
The issue was also raised by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on October 31. Zelenskyy thanked Ankara for supporting Ukraine's sovereignty and efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
Europeans Challenge Lavrov
The Atlanta gathering exposed deep divisions between Moscow and European governments, with Lavrov's presence prompting several delegations to refuse participation in the traditional G20 family photograph. The photograph was ultimately canceled.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Lavrov of presenting false narratives about the war during the discussions.
Kallas told reporters that Russia did not appear ready for peace negotiations, pointing to the continued intensity of attacks on Ukraine.
Lavrov, meanwhile, criticized what he called Europe's "arrogant boycott" and praised the Trump administration's willingness to engage with Moscow.
Rubio said the US remained committed to exploring a diplomatic solution, describing the war as devastating for both countries.
He pointed to Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and rising civilian casualties, while also citing the heavy Russian military losses. He estimated that around 20,000 Russians were being killed each month.
"It's a very deadly and destructive war," Rubio said, warning that every additional month of fighting would make the eventual reconstruction of Ukraine more difficult.
He described Washington's central objective as determining whether it could use its contacts with both sides to facilitate an end to the conflict.
No G20 Consensus
The two-day ministerial ended without a joint communique, as disagreements over Ukraine, the Middle East, trade, and maritime security prevented the world's largest economies from reaching consensus.
Instead, the US presidency issued a chairman's statement outlining shared priorities, including energy and food security, critical minerals, supply chains, and freedom of navigation. It made no mention of Russia, Ukraine, or the war between them.
"I wouldn't pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems," Rubio said.
The Atlanta meeting was the final high-level G20 gathering before the leaders' summit in Miami in mid-December.
Rubio said he would not rule out an invitation for Zelenskyy to attend, although he stressed that the decision rested with Trump.

articles.title: Most Ukrainian brigades are short of troops. One that filled its ranks is helping push Russia back in Operation Vivaldi.
articles.body:
- Ukrainian brigades tend to suffer from low manning and equipment shortages
- One key brigade bucked the trend
- The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade says its main units are nearly fully manned, with tanks and infantry fighting vehicles to match
In four months of deft maneuver, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps cleared Russian troops from 277 sq km of northern Donetsk Oblast, inflicting—according to the corps—8,000 casualties on the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies and chasing the armies back across a key terrain feature, the Zherebets River.
There are many reasons for the success of the 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi—which the corps declared finished on 19 October, though elements reportedly keep pushing across the Zherebets to the river's eastern bank.
But one reason is becoming clearer. Bucking a worrying trend, the 3rd Army Corps under its former commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi actually managed to nearly fill out at least one of its five line brigades. The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade's main units—three infantry and tank battalions, which make up around half the overall brigade—have filled between 95% and 100% of their allotted billets, the brigade says.
That means the brigade rolls into battle with as many as 1,500 infantry and vehicle crew. (A battalion typically has around 500 personnel.)
Ukraine may already be pushing Operation Vivaldi across the Zherebets River. It’s a risky gamble
That's highly unusual. Almost all of the roughly 150 ground combat brigades in the Ukrainian armed forces have too few infantry. “Ukraine faces manpower shortage and still does not have a single brigade that is fully manned,” analyst Giorgi Revishvili wrote in June. Some brigades are effectively battalions given their stubbornly low manning.
The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade—commanded by Maj. Volodymyr Fokin—may be one exception to that truism. And if you believe the brigade's own claims, the unit not only has nearly all of its allotted infantry, it also has an abundance of heavy equipment including American-made M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicles and German-made Leopard tanks. (It's unclear whether they're Leopard 1s or heavier Leopard 2s.) The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade's line battalions should possess around 90 armored vehicles between them.
"3rd Army Corps is built different," observer Moklasen quipped. The corps grew out of the 3rd Assault Brigade, whose soldiers described it as a new army modeled on the freedom-loving Cossacks rather than on the regulations.
Turnaround
The brigade wasn't always so fit. Indeed, as recently as a year ago it was just 17% manned and lacked heavy equipment, the brigade says, making it more typical of the younger Ukrainian brigades including the notoriously "poor" 29th Heavy Mechanized Brigade.
The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade stood up in 2022 as a lightly equipped territorial defense brigade, transferred to the army in 2024 as a mechanized brigade and thereafter underwent reorganization to the new vehicle-centric heavy mechanized structure.
But it took Fokin's strong leadership to actually fill out that structure, the brigade stated. Fokin and his staff "started changing things instead of looking for excuses," according to the brigade's official Telegram account.
"Within just one year, the unit has risen to the top ranks in terms of enemy attrition, mine-laying, artillery operations, air defense, unmanned ground systems, and reconnaissance. Among heavy mechanized brigades, it has held the top spot for three consecutive months."
“We were told brigade couldn’t be saved”: Ukraine’s 125th grew its manning 430% and won back 1,500 absent soldiers in one year
Success bred success. Increasingly confident in the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade's leadership, some 1,500 troops who had gone absent without leave returned and rejoined the fight, according to the brigade. That helped drive a 430% increase in unit manning, by the brigade's count, until its main units were essentially fully manned.
"The unit no longer fights with unarmed personnel," the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade reported. "Today, the brigade is active and conducting successful offensive operations. Its arsenal ranges from unmanned systems, unmanned ground vehicles and electronic warfare assets to armored personnel carriers, armored combat vehicles and artillery. It also boasts high-quality medical support, robust rear-echelon logistics, and a cadre of professional commanders."
Brigade troopers and their vehicles and drones underwent a baptism of fire as part of Operation Vivaldi. Robots led the way, but armored vehicles and infantry followed. The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade and the other assault and mechanized brigades under the 3rd Army Corps banner advanced steadily, exploiting gaps in the overextended 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies and pushing back the bigger Russian formations.
"Operating as part of the corps, our units are once again liberating Ukrainian territory, safeguarding their personnel and continuing to evolve," the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade stated. Its success, the brigade says, began with strong leadership that inspired confidence in its rank-and-file soldiers—and motivated them to stay and fight.
Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman

articles.title: Russian airstrike destroys Kramatorsk city council building that survived 2014 occupation
articles.body:
The Kramatorsk City Council executive committee building following a Russian airstrike on Oct. 31, 2026. (Oleksandr Honcharenko/Facebook)
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
A Russian airstrike destroyed the Kramatorsk City Council's executive committee building in Donetsk Oblast on Oct. 31, local authorities reported.
The building, located on Peace Square in central Kramatorsk, survived the city's occupation by Russian-backed militants in 2014 and its subsequent liberation by Ukrainian forces.
"An hour ago, Russia destroyed the central building of Ukrainian statehood in Kramatorsk with an airstrike," Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the city's military administration, wrote on Facebook, referring to the city council's executive committee.
Honcharenko described the building as a symbol of the city's history and identity.
"They can destroy a building, scorch our land and steal our memories. But they cannot destroy our right to a future," he wrote.
The building had previously sustained damage during a Russian airstrike on the city centre in March 2026.
Information about casualties from that strike was not immediately available.

articles.title: Distaste for Russian diplomat forces US to cancel G-20 photo session
articles.body:
Distaste for Russian diplomat forces US to cancel G-20 photo session
Michael Crowley
- US-hosted G-20 talks in Atlanta began badly when a group photo was cancelled after some diplomats refused to pose with Russia’s Sergey Lavrov over the Ukraine war.
- Marco Rubio cancelled the photo to avoid distraction. Poland’s Radoslaw Sikorski called it “the right decision”, while US officials said the meeting should stay focused on substance.
- The row reflects wider G-20 tensions over Russia’s role. Rubio said the world faces “interconnected economic and geopolitical crises”, including energy, food supplies and freedom of navigation.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A US-hosted gathering of foreign ministers got off to an awkward start on Oct 30 when a planned group photo was cancelled after some diplomats refused to pose alongside Russia’s top diplomat, Sergey Lavrov.
The ministers are in Atlanta for a two-day meeting of the Group of 20 (G-20), a forum of major nations that seek to coordinate global economic and political policy.
Russia is a longtime member of the group, which also includes Brazil, Japan, Saudi Arabia, China, Japan and several European states. But many European diplomats believe that Russian officials like Lavrov should be shunned over Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters in Atlanta, Poland’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radoslaw Sikorski, said the photo cancellation was “the right decision”.
“I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov,” he added.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the event, made the decision to cancel the traditional photo, according to a senior US official. Another US official said that after it became clear that some attendees were unwilling to participate in a joint photo, Rubio acted so the matter would not distract from substantive issues at the event.
Lavrov has been under US sanctions since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. He led his country’s talks with the United States ostensibly meant to avert the war, although Biden administration officials later concluded that those talks were not in good faith.
After President Donald Trump encouraged President Vladimir Putin of Russia in September to attend a planned December meeting of G-20 leaders in Miami, 14 senators from both parties sent a letter to the White House urging that neither Putin “nor any sanctioned Russian officials be permitted at upcoming G-20 events”.
Trump’s envoys have conducted extensive talks with Putin in an effort to broker a peace agreement for Ukraine. In their letter, the senators warned Trump against “legitimising and normalising a government that continues to attack Ukrainian civilian targets every day”.
Asked in October about Lavrov’s expected attendance, Rubio – who as a US senator was a fierce critic of Russia but has softened his public stance since joining the Trump administration – seemed lukewarm.
“Well, the Russians are invited to be a part of the G-20,” Rubio said. “The president made that decision. So obviously they’re going to be represented at each of these summits.”
Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, mocked the dispute over the photo on Telegram. Citing reports that Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, had been among the diplomats most opposed to joining a group picture with Lavrov, she called him afraid and posted a photograph of a working session at the event that showed the two men, seated at a large rectangular table with other ministers, in the same frame.
The photographic drama was not unprecedented. G-20 foreign ministers also skipped their traditional group photographs in 2022, 2023 and 2025 amid tensions over Russia’s participation in the gatherings, although South African officials officially attributed the 2025 omission to scheduling difficulties.
Russia’s finance minister was also excluded from an equivalent photo session at a Sept 1 meeting of his G-20 counterparts in North Carolina.
Trump officials said they expected the Atlanta gathering to focus on economic issues, including global energy supplies and the related question of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has menaced shipping since the United States and Israel launched a war against the country in February.
Speaking at an opening session on the morning of Oct 30, Rubio said the world was “at a critical moment”.
“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises” that threaten the global economic order, Rubio said. The G-20 needs to work together, he added, to address disruptions to global energy and food supplies and “to freedom of navigation itself.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

articles.title: Ukraine and NATO to deepen cooperation on innovative technologies
articles.body:
Ukraine and NATO to deepen cooperation on innovative technologies
The Ministry of Defense reported this, according to Ukrinform.
The Defense Ministry noted that this is the first agreement of its kind between DIANA and a NATO partner country. It lays the groundwork for closer cooperation between the innovation ecosystems of Ukraine and the Alliance.
“Ukraine has gained unique experience in rapidly developing, testing, and improving technologies in modern warfare. For its part, DIANA gives Ukraine access to NATO’s defense expertise and infrastructure, helping promising technologies move from idea to practical application. This will allow Ukrainian developers to gain a deeper understanding of the Alliance’s standards, open up new avenues for testing their own solutions, and help remove obstacles to scaling them up,” the ministry said.
The signing of the memorandum will provide additional funding for joint Ukraine-NATO projects, the Defense Ministry emphasized.
In addition, the memorandum will contribute to:
- building a comprehensive defense innovation system that combines the cataloging, testing, and adoption of technological solutions with deeper cooperation with NATO and other international partners;
- continuing to build and develop a catalog of innovative defense technologies that covers, in particular, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), electronic warfare (EW) systems, radars, and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs).
The catalog is to contain coordinated information on existing and promising solutions, their level of readiness, test results and potential applications, and will be used to identify priorities for technology development, procurement and scaling.
Other benefits include:
- deeper engagement with NATO institutions, including the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) and DIANA, ensuring that Ukrainian combat experience and the needs of the Defense Forces of Ukraine are taken into account when setting technological priorities, preparing and announcing innovation competitions, supporting projects, and testing solutions, including in Ukraine;
- synchronization of the innovative technology catalogs of Ukraine and NATO member states;
- exchange of information to strengthen situational awareness, identify common needs, and plan joint competitions, testing, and technology adoption.
The ministry said that the consistent implementation of these tasks would strengthen Ukraine’s ability to influence the development of NATO’s innovation priorities and secure partner support in line with the needs of the Defense Forces.
The synchronization of catalogs and joint identification of technological priorities will lay the groundwork for systematic situational awareness, long-term planning and forecasting of the development of defense technologies.
The Defense Ministry also recalled that it is working on implementing the NATO Status of Forces Agreement (NATO SOFA). The document defines the legal status of the armed forces of States Parties while they are in the territory of another State Party. It regulates entry and exit, criminal and disciplinary jurisdiction, compensation for damage, and customs and tax regulation.
As Ukrinform reported, Jacqueline Borsboom, NATO Support and Procurement Agency's Director of Support to Operations, said that NATO will allow Ukraine to procure weapons, ammunition and military equipment through its centralized procurement agency, which will help Kyiv obtain the weapons it needs faster and at lower cost.

articles.title: 'Politicisation of energy flows harmful': Jaishankar calls for diversified supply chains at G20
articles.body:
Jaishankar speaks at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, calling for diversified supply chains and the de-politicisation of energy markets
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday called for reducing political interference in energy markets and diversifying global supply chains, saying disruptions were placing a disproportionate burden on developing countries.Speaking about the message he delivered at G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said the discussions covered geopolitical conflicts, energy and food security, and resilient supply chains.“Look, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications,” ANI quoted him as saying. He added that “there are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway.”On energy security, Jaishankar warned against disruptions in fuel distribution and their impact on developing economies. “This distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful,” he said, adding that “the Global South was bearing the brunt of the energy shortages and that something needs to be done.”He also flagged risks to food security, citing disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea regions.
At the meeting's concluding session on supply chains, Jaishankar called for wider diversification of manufacturing and production across countries. “Today we need more diversified supply chains,” he said, advocating “more globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing.”In a post on X after the session, he said securing supply chains was central to the global economy's well-being and called on the G20 to promote “the right to industrialise” and resist “predatory practices”.“Diversification and de-risking, including in connectivity, is the key to supply chain resilience, threatened by pandemics, conflicts, climate events and mishaps,” he said.
Jaishankar also urged the grouping to work towards the “de-politicisation of markets” and prevent the concentration of production and resources in a few geographies.US secretary of state Marco Rubio, who hosted the meeting, also stressed the need to secure critical trade routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb, and strengthen supply chains for critical minerals.On the sidelines, Jaishankar attended a Quad foreign ministers' meeting with Rubio and his Japanese and Australian counterparts. He also met Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov, with discussions covering the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf situation and multilateral issues.

articles.title: Binance says it covered 90% of cyberattack losses as FBI links theft to North Korea
articles.body:
Cryptocurrency platform Binance has said it has used company money to buy tokens to replenish 90 percent of $6.3 billion stolen in a huge hacking attack, as the FBI links the theft to North Korea.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, said the remaining 10 percent of tokens are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
The company said it has set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack.
Binance said Friday it was working to resolve what it called a "complex attack" with several "points of breach."
North Korea link
Later on Saturday, the FBI said that North Korea was behind the theft.
"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the US law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the incident, but said in its latest update they were on track to resume on Sunday.
The attack on Binance came as many observers expressed worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

articles.title: Clearing the shadow: Celebrated American Col. David ‘Mickey’ Marcus’s true contribution to the IDF
articles.body:
Yael Driver is the daughter of the late Maj.-Gen. Shlomo Shamir, who recruited Colonel David “Mickey” Marcus in January 1948. She maintains that her father was the person closest to the celebrated American army veteran, from the latter’s recruitment and arrival in what was then British Mandate Palestine, until his accidental death on June 11, 1948. Her parents maintained contact with his widow, Emma Marcus, well into the 1960s.
Driver hopes to clear up some misconceptions, even well-meaning ones, related to Marcus’s recruitment, his status as Israel’s first major-General, the battle for Jerusalem, and his actual contribution to the fledgling Israel Defense Forces.
David “Mickey” Marcus (nom de guerre – Mickey Stone) was a rare Jewish graduate of America’s prestigious West Point Military Academy. Born to a secular Jewish family in New York’s Lower East Side, he served in the US Army during World War II. After the war, he served as Chief of the War Crimes Branch of the US War Department and was involved in the Nuremberg Trials, which prosecuted Nazi war criminals.
Driver recounted a conversation documented by her father in which he mentioned talking with Marcus during their flight to Palestine. Shamir asked Marcus why he agreed to become an adviser to the newly created IDF. Marcus’s reply: “Because I have Abraham’s blood in my veins.”
Shamir (then Rabinowicz) served during World War II as an officer in the Jewish Brigade of the British Army, which consisted largely of Jewish volunteers from British-ruled Palestine. After being discharged from the British Army in the spring of 1946, he was appointed by the Haganah and the Jewish national institutions in Palestine as head of the Haganah Mission in the US.
At that time, David Ben-Gurion was head of the Jewish Agency, later to become leader of the provisional government, and then Israel’s first prime minister.
In October 1947, while working in the US, Shamir was tasked by Ben-Gurion with identifying an experienced American general who could serve as an adviser to the fledgling Jewish army.
Shamir’s six years of service in the British Army had exposed him to the workings of a regular army. This provided him and his brothers-in-arms with experience and understanding that a significant number of soldiers in the fledgling IDF, who had not served in a regular army, were lacking.
In November 1947, while searching for suitable advisers, Shamir met Marcus, then a lawyer in New York.
Based on her father’s correspondence, documents, and photographs, Driver confirmed with confidence that Marcus indeed contributed significantly to the success of the War of Independence but not in the way that the star-studded film about his life, Cast a Giant Shadow, implies.
She has suggested that the most important contribution of Marcus was helping to convert a specific but important group of IDF soldiers with no experience in a regular army, and with little respect for authority, rank or military discipline, to accept basic regular army structures and codes of behavior and thereby helping to turn the fledgling IDF into what is today considered one of the most effective and successful armies in the world.
The search for an American General
In December 1946, Shamir was in the US as head of the Haganah Mission. World War II had only recently ended, and the dramatic UN resolution of November 29, 1947, in which the majority of nations voted for a Jewish homeland in Palestine, was yet to take place. But the soon-to-be Israelis were not waiting around as the surrounding Arab nations were openly gearing up for an invasion.
After being summoned back to Palestine for consultation with Ben-Gurion, Shamir consulted with Moshe Sharett, head of the Jewish Agency’s political department, who was stationed in New York. Sharett contacted Murray Gurfein, a distinguished lawyer and federal jurist who, immediately after World War II, had served as an assistant to the US chief counsel at the Nuremberg Trials, where he interacted with Marcus.
This is how Shamir, Sharett, Gurfein, and Marcus ended up having lunch together at a New York restaurant. Within days, Shamir and Marcus reviewed a list of 24 candidates, which was whittled down to five preferred candidates, and eventually down to one: Maj.-Gen. Ralph C. Smith.
Smith was not Jewish and had no connection to the Jewish community. He was a military educator with a storied background and extensive combat experience. He was taught to fly by Orville Wright, of the Wright Brothers. He participated in the Pancho Villa Expedition and was a veteran of World War I and World War II.
He oversaw intensive training for thousands of World War II soldiers, earning him an American Legion of Merit and a French Légion d’honneur award. He also helped create CARE packages for war-torn Europe.
Shamir and Marcus flew to San Francisco to meet with Smith and later drew up an official letter from the Jewish Agency offering him a job as military adviser at a salary of $1,000 per month, plus expenses.
Even though Smith received US government approval for employment as an adviser, Smith’s army pension could have been lost, and he declined the offer.
Marcus, by contrast, had no such pension issue, and when no other suitable adviser could be secured, Marcus accepted the job. His salary was to be $750 per month, plus expenses.
The struggle for unity of command
Marcus arrived in Palestine at the beginning of 1948, still months away from Israel’s independence. One of the first things he noticed about the pre-state, paramilitary defense organizations was that although some soldiers had experience from the British and other foreign armies, others were much more relaxed and informal about military procedures and discipline than would be expected in a regular army.
This was especially true of those in the Palmach’s ranks. When met with the informal nature of these soldiers, Marcus commented, “Every platoon commander is a general.”
It is estimated that about 30,000 Jewish soldiers were veterans of the British Army. This compares to about 4,000 to 5,000 soldiers who were associated with the Palmach, the military group established in 1941 within the Haganah.
Driver describes this latter group of soldiers as “courageous, loyal, and ready to sacrifice their lives,” but said that in contrast to those with regular army experience, they had no concept of rank or structure. They operated more like small, friendly, interchangeable groups, where one day a soldier would be in one group and the next day would belong to a different one.
To help instill basic regular army concepts, Marcus brought with him some US Army manuals on military training, which he adapted to meet the situation at hand. Others had them translated into Hebrew. These later formed the basis for future IDF manuals used by commanders today.
So what did these informal Hebrew-speakers think of the new outsider? Not much to start with, according to Driver, but he quickly won them over.
“There is no doubt that his personality, smiling face, and ability to talk in a friendly way to anybody were contributing factors to his being accepted even by those who didn’t have any respect for military discipline,” Driver explained. She added that he was physically fit and impressed the younger soldiers with his abilities.
The credit for lifting the siege on Jerusalem
Marcus left Palestine at the end of March 1948 and returned to his wife in New York. He came back to Palestine once more in early May 1948. This was just days before the British officially left and the State of Israel was proclaimed an independent country.
From the beginning, Jerusalem was to be the new State of Israel’s capital, but it was under siege by the surrounding Arab countries, having limited food and water supplies, with the threat of starvation being very real.
“Securing Jerusalem and thereby ensuring its recognition as the capital of the new State of Israel was both of crucial importance and urgent. This is manifested by Chief of Operations Yigael Yadin’s telegram ‘at any cost, Jerusalem,’” noted Driver.
The 1966 film Cast a Giant Shadow was a dramatized version of Marcus’s life, starring Kirk Douglas, Yul Brynner, John Wayne, and other notable American stars. A main focus of the movie was the creation of the road that lifted the siege on Jerusalem and enabled convoys of trucks with food and supplies to reach the city.
On May 28, 1948, Ben-Gurion appointed Marcus the “Supreme Commander of the Jerusalem Front and general” with permission to nominate his own staff. Driver maintains that “this appointment was a declarative one. It tragically turned out to be for only two weeks.”
Driver explained that the main road to Jerusalem was controlled at Latrun by the Arab Legion. Therefore, attempts were made to create a new road to break through to Jerusalem, bypassing the enemy. One first attempt was Derech Ha’ayalot (Deer Road), a dirt road forged by the Palmach’s Har’el Brigade.
But this small road was impassable for convoys of heavy vehicles needed to deliver the required amount of supplies to the besieged city.
The second road was Route 7, named after its creators, the 7th Brigade, which was wider and able to accommodate large convoys of vehicles with enough supplies to alleviate the struggling Jerusalem residents. It was also referred to as the Burma Road, after the famous road used by the Allies in World War II to transport supplies from Burma to China.
“This was the usable road that enabled the lifting of the siege on Jerusalem,” Driver said.
In his book …At any cost – to Jerusalem, published in Hebrew in 1994, Shamir attested that Marcus did not participate in the process of planning or building of Route 7. Marcus, having been assigned a Hebrew-speaking secretary, did not speak or write in Hebrew and did not appoint his own staff.
“It is therefore hard to credit him with being a commander, especially during wartime,” Driver said. However, she described Marcus as “a most important unifier and adviser rather than a commander.”
Was Marcus Israel’s first major-general?
So can Marcus be credited as Israel’s first major-general? Driver states that a clear answer is complicated, and one needs to be aware of the full context.
Driver pointed out that when Marcus was appointed to his position, the IDF had not yet introduced formal ranks. Ben-Gurion only determined such ranks two weeks later, by which time Marcus was no longer alive.
In fact, Appendix 1 to IDF General Staff Ordinance No. 10, dated August 11, 1948, announced that the appointment of the first 12 IDF officers to be assigned the rank of major-general would take effect retroactively from August 1, 1948. Marcus was not one of these.
“It’s important to understand that although Marcus was appointed Supreme Commander of the Jerusalem Front on May 28, 1948, as an American citizen, and as an ex-officer in the US Army, he was forbidden to swear allegiance to another flag and officially serve in a non-US Army,” Driver elaborated.
In other words, “he was not allowed to receive an official IDF position even if it were offered, which explains why he was granted the official rank only after his death.”
“All this explains why the rank of major-general was awarded to Marcus posthumously, 14 months after his death,” Driver said. “The announcement about it appeared shortly before August 16, 1949.”
She further explained: “This supports the notion that granting Marcus the rank of major-general in May 1948 was a declarative and symbolic act on Ben-Gurion’s part.
“It was Ben-Gurion who put into effect the concept of unity of command on local commanders, for whom a regular army arrangement was alien and unacceptable,” she noted. “Ben-Gurion achieved this by using a professional figure accepted as neutral, i.e., not a veteran of the British Army and not from the Haganah.
“It is most likely that the granting of this rank to Marcus accelerated the acceptance of the principle of ‘unity of command,’ a principle that Marcus himself emphasized in his very first lecture to the top echelon of the fledgling IDF,” she explained.
“In conclusion, there is nothing wrong with viewing Marcus as the IDF’s first major-general, but it is important to be aware of what lay behind the appointment and what it actually meant in practice.”
Driver was proud to have received permission to visit West Point Cemetery, where she paid respects at Marcus’s grave, calling it a “very moving” experience.
For her, the important thing is ensuring that the memory of people like Marcus, and the other brave men and women who fought and worked for the revival of an independent Jewish nation, are properly credited and remembered for their critical contributions.■

articles.title: Former Mossad agent assisted Flavio Bolsonaro's escape from Brazil via Argentina - report
articles.body:
A former Mossad agent who became a naturalized US citizen assisted Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, in escaping Brazil in violation of a judicial order barring him from leaving the country.
CNN Brazil revealed the operation on Friday, citing findings from a security agency investigation in Brazil.
According to the report, the operation was planned prior to the second round of the presidential election and involved assistance from figures in Argentina and the United States.
Former Mossad agent arrived prior to elections
According to the investigation, the former Israeli intelligence officer, whose identity has not been disclosed, arrived in Brazil on October 19, six days before the second round of the presidential election. He accompanied Bolsonaro from the capital, Brasília, to the border with Argentina and remained in the vehicle with him during the border crossing.
Brazilian investigators identified two commercial vans that crossed the Tancredo Neves Bridge connecting Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil to Puerto Iguazú in Argentina via security camera footage on Tuesday.
Bolsonaro and the former Mossad agent traveled in one of the vehicles, while his wife and two daughters traveled in the second. One driver was identified as a former municipal council member from Foz do Iguaçu, and the second driver was his son.
Private jet and Argentine assistance
After crossing the border, the family boarded a Gulfstream G400 executive jet operated by the Argentine airline Baires Fly. The aircraft took off for the United States, refueled in Guayaquil, Ecuador, and landed Wednesday morning at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami.
According to a report in The New York Times, Jason Miller, a political strategist close to US President Donald Trump, helped arrange the aircraft.
Concurrently, the Argentine newspaper Clarín reported that Santiago Caputo, a top advisor to Argentine President Javier Milei, arrived in the border area to oversee the operation and prevent documentation of the crossing.
Election defeat and judicial order
The escape followed Bolsonaro's defeat to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of elections on October 25.
Following the election, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the confiscation of Bolsonaro's passports and barred him from leaving the country. The senator is under investigation for suspected money laundering, including a case involving gambling platforms and another regarding the funding of a film about his father. The allegations have not been proven in court.
The Federal Police stated that no official record was found of the senator's departure through Brazilian border control checkpoints.
Diplomatic crisis between nations
Brazilian government officials described the event as a planned international rescue mission, internally dubbed Operation Alba. According to officials, spreading misleading information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was part of the preparation. The Brazilian Foreign Ministry summoned Argentina's representative to demand clarifications regarding potential involvement by the Milei administration.
Simultaneously, 25 Democratic lawmakers in the United States demanded that the Trump administration explain whether US diplomatic resources were used to assist in the escape.
The Federal Police in Brazil is considering applying to the Supreme Court to freeze Bolsonaro's assets and bank accounts. At this stage, allegations of foreign government involvement and assistance from the former Mossad agent are based on investigation findings published in the media, not a final judicial ruling.

articles.title: Rift between El-Sayed and pro-Israel Democratic primary rival puts Michigan Jews on edge
articles.body:
An 11th-hour public feud between Michigan Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his pro-Israel former primary rival is further exacerbating tensions between Jewish voters and the nominee ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.
US Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the race for the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed this summer, had previously endorsed her former competitor and was set to join him at a rally Sunday in the crucial final days of campaigning. Michigan is locked in a tight race that could help determine which party controls the Senate.
Instead of a show of unity, Stevens is now forcefully criticizing El-Sayed for his recent criticism of Israel and for not condemning a PAC ad, made by an outside group to boost his campaign, that blamed Israel for rising grocery prices. El-Sayed has shot back, invoking Stevens’ close relationship with the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC.
Stevens, who represents a large Jewish district in suburban Detroit, unloaded on El-Sayed Friday in a series of interviews with The New York Times published early Saturday morning.
On social media Friday, Stevens said she expected El-Sayed to condemn the ad soon, paid for by Rebellion PAC, a project of far-left commentator Cenk Uygur. El-Sayed had earlier distanced himself from the ad but had not commented on its content.
“We are not going to say that the cost of groceries is because of Jews and the Jewish state,” Stevens told the NYT, adding, “Maybe it is what you want people to believe.” She stopped short of formally rescinding her endorsement of El-Sayed.
Much of Democratic establishment coalesces behind El-Sayed
The feud comes at a moment when much of the Democratic establishment has coalesced behind El-Sayed in the key Senate race, even as deep concerns remain among many traditionally Democratic Jewish voters. Stevens’ fiancée, Jewish Democratic megadonor Jason Turkish, said this week he would vote for Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Stevens told the NYT she met with a rabbi before their wedding and is mulling converting to Judaism.
In a statement sent to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency and other outlets Friday, El-Sayed accused Stevens of “relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” He also said he had already “defeated” spending “from outside corporations and AIPAC” on Stevens' behalf.
El-Sayed did not mention the Uygur ad, nor another ad - this one produced by his campaign - that featured a brief clip of far-right commentator and anti-Israel voice Tucker Carlson announcing he wouldn’t vote for Rogers. Stevens had publicly urged El-Sayed to take down the Carlson ad, which the campaign had aired on conservative TV channels.
The El-Sayed campaign has dropped Stevens’ name from its description of Sunday’s planned Detroit church event, which is now scheduled to feature Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. USA Today and other outlets have reported that El-Sayed’s campaign has asked Stevens to stay away from all future events.
Stevens and Turkish did not return a JTA request for comment.
In her social media statement Friday prior to El-Sayed’s response, Stevens had outlined Jewish constituent concerns about El-Sayed, noting that he himself has used rhetoric akin to blaming Michigan’s financial ills on Israel.
“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care,” Stevens wrote. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
Both Turkish, in an earlier JTA interview from a Rogers event, and Stevens, to the NYT, said their final breaking point with El-Sayed came after a recent debate in which the nominee had declined to say whether Israel or Iran posed a bigger threat to the United States.
El-Sayed condemns Hasan Piker comments
El-Sayed on Friday did condemn a separate comment from anti-Israel streamer and former campaign ally Hasan Piker, who is Uygur’s nephew. In a stream this week, Piker had compared the heavily Jewish Detroit suburb of West Bloomfield to a “KKK neighborhood,” adding, “The supremacist attitude underlying their worldview is identical.”
In a statement to Jewish Insider about Piker’s comments, El-Sayed noted he grew up near West Bloomfield and stated, “Comparing Jewish Michiganders to the Ku Klux Klan is utterly inappropriate and flat-out wrong.”
Meanwhile, Republicans are jumping at the Jewish divide. Rogers, a former congressman, has seized on the intraparty feud to appeal to Jewish voters who had supported Stevens in the primary. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump called Jews who back El-Sayed “crazy,” leading to condemnation from some Jewish leaders.

articles.title: Iran’s energy and environmental crises: The promise of a free Iran - opinion
articles.body:
Iran holds some of the world’s largest oil and natural gas reserves, yet millions of Iranians are struggling with energy shortages, inefficient industries, and severe air pollution.
During periods of natural gas shortages, particularly in winter, power plants and industrial facilities have increasingly relied on highly polluting fuels such as mazut, a heavy fuel oil that contributes significantly to air pollution.
The problem is compounded by winter temperature inversions, which trap pollutants near the ground and intensify air pollution in major cities.
These interconnected failures carry enormous human and economic costs. According to Iran’s own Health Ministry, nearly 59,000 deaths were attributed to air pollution in the Iranian year ending March 2025, with an estimated economic loss of $17.2 billion.
Behind this crisis lies nearly 47 years of governance under the Islamic regime that has failed to translate the country’s natural wealth into public health, energy security, and sustainable economic prosperity.
The Islamic Republic has repeatedly subordinated environmental protection and sustainable development to political, ideological, and institutional interests. Decades of inadequate investment, weak regulatory oversight, and a lack of institutional accountability have allowed these systemic failures to persist largely unchecked.
Recently, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi emphasized the environmental damage caused by American and Israeli military strikes. Armed conflicts can undoubtedly cause ecological harm, deserving independent scientific investigation.
But Iran’s environmental and energy crises long predate these conflicts. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been a major contributor to Iran’s environmental degradation through its extensive military and economic activities, including environmentally destructive infrastructure projects, encroachment into ecologically protected areas, and activities that have undermined independent environmental oversight.
Environmental accountability cannot be selective. A regime that has spent nearly 47 years exploiting Iran’s natural resources to serve its political and ideological interests cannot credibly portray itself as a defender of the environment while ignoring the destruction associated with its own policies.
Redefining national prosperity
Iran’s energy insecurity and environmental deterioration are closely connected. Inefficient electricity generation, aging infrastructure, inadequate natural gas management, and the combustion of highly polluting fuels contribute to the pollution crisis while undermining industrial productivity.
Iran’s natural resources should serve its people rather than sustain institutional inefficiency and political privilege. Achieving that transformation will demand accountable institutions, coordinated environmental and energy policies, industrial modernization, and international partnerships.
The Iran Prosperity Project, developing a road map for Iran’s reconstruction after the Islamic Republic under the leadership of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, recognizes that environmental recovery, energy security, and economic revitalization must advance together.
Modernizing Iran’s energy infrastructure, improving natural gas management, and diversifying electricity generation are essential to addressing chronic energy shortages and reducing reliance on highly polluting fuels.
At the same time, strengthening environmental regulations, improving pollution monitoring, and investing in cleaner technologies can help restore air quality and protect public health. Together, these efforts provide the foundation for sustainable industrial and economic development.
Industrial revitalization offers an opportunity to transform Iran’s outdated production systems into competitive, efficient, and environmentally responsible industries.
Environmental protection should be integrated into industrial modernization rather than treated as a competing priority. Cleaner production processes, modern pollution controls, and energy-efficient manufacturing can reduce environmental impacts while improving productivity.
Modernizing public transportation, introducing cleaner vehicle technologies, and encouraging industrial competition could improve urban air quality while creating opportunities for technological innovation and skilled employment.
The objective should not be to choose between industrial growth and environmental protection, but to build an economy in which modernization advances both.
International cooperation opportunities
Rebuilding Iran’s energy, industrial, and environmental systems will require investment, scientific expertise, and international cooperation.
Pahlavi’s vision, reflected in the proposed Cyrus Accords, offers opportunities for partnerships based on technological progress, economic development, and mutual prosperity.
The Cyrus Accords could help translate renewed Iranian-Israeli relations into practical cooperation across these critical sectors.
Such engagement could provide a foundation for future collaboration in clean energy, infrastructure modernization, advanced manufacturing, environmental technologies, and pollution control.
Joint research, technology partnerships, and professional exchanges could combine Israeli experience with Iran’s substantial scientific and engineering capabilities, developing solutions tailored to the country’s economic and environmental needs.
These partnerships could also demonstrate how scientific cooperation can overcome decades of hostility imposed by the Islamic regime, restoring friendship and delivering tangible benefits to both nations.
After nearly 47 years of failed governance under the Islamic regime, Iranians deserve a country where abundant energy resources power competitive industries instead of recurring shortages, where economic progress supports environmental protection, and where scientific cooperation replaces ideological hostility.
Making Iran’s skies breathable, its energy reliable, and its industries competitive would be powerful measures of a free Iran’s renewal.
Dr. Aidin Panahi is an energy and industrial policy expert, author, and advisor to the Iran Prosperity Project. Follow him on X: @Aidin_FreeIran
Dr. Bahram Vahedi is a water and environmental researcher, strategist, author, and advisor to the Iran Prosperity Project. Follow him on X: @VahediBahram

articles.title: UN Human Rights staff member dies in Houthi custody after arbitrary detention of two years
articles.body:
A Yemeni staff member of the UN Human Rights Office has died in Houthi custody after being arbitrarily detained for more than two years, the UN human rights chief said on Saturday, calling for an independent investigation and the release of other detained personnel.
Mohammad el Shami had been held by the Houthi militant group since June 6, 2024, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Tuerk said in a statement.
His family said they had been informed of his death only recently, more than a month after it occurred, and had received no explanation of the cause or circumstances, Tuerk said.
Tuerk called for a prompt, independent and thorough investigation, and demanded the immediate and unconditional release of all other UN personnel held by the Houthis, including seven colleagues from his office, as well as humanitarian workers and civil society members.
Yemen's prime minister condemned the death, held the Houthis fully responsible and called for those responsible to be held accountable. He said more than 70 UN employees and dozens of humanitarian workers remained detained.
Houthis allege detainies part of US-Israeli spy network
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis. The group has said those detained were part of a spy network working for the United States and Israel. The group has also accused humanitarian organizations of using their work as cover for intelligence activities, without providing evidence.
The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. The conflict has since divided the country, with the Houthis holding Sanaa and much of the north and northwest, while government-aligned forces control much of the south and east.

articles.title: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
articles.body:
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.
In a prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.
Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.
Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.
The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.
Defending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.
He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.
Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians in Poland who seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”
He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev had joined the opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.
He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”
He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.
On Saturday, the European Commission urged Nawrocki to approve the new judges who were nominated by parliament, so the court could function in line with the constitution and EU law.
The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.
However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.
Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.
The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”
Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.

Heroin and cocaine not produced in Ukraine – police

“Heroin and cocaine are not produced in Ukraine. Heroin has generally been smuggled into the country, with most of it passing through in transit,” he said.
Nikitin noted that law enforcement officers, with the assistance of the Prosecutor General’s Office and National Police leadership, are currently documenting the activities of groups involved in smuggling cocaine into Ukraine.
“While we seize synthetic drugs in quantities measured in tons during our operations, cocaine is seized in much smaller batches. But it is present in Ukraine,” he added.
According to Nikitin, one reason synthetic drugs have flooded Ukraine’s drug market is that their production requires minimal investment while generating enormous profits from sales to end consumers.
“Another reason is how easy they are to produce. Unlike growing plants, there is no need to wait for a certain period or depend on specific weather conditions. All that is needed is an inconspicuous premises, usually an abandoned building, and precursors brought into Ukraine disguised as ordinary products,” the law enforcement official said.
He noted that anonymous sales also contribute to the popularity of synthetic drugs in Ukraine, as they are distributed through Telegram channels, allowing buyers and sellers to remain out of direct contact.
Nikitin said cannabis is also present in Ukraine, but because its cultivation requires specific conditions, it cannot be produced on the same scale as synthetic drugs.

articles.title: Evidence of what may be world’s oldest shipwreck found in underwater excavations off Turkish isle
articles.body:
Evidence of what may be the world's oldest shipwreck was discovered off the coast of Kekova, Turkish Tourism and Culture Minister Mehmet Ersoy announced on X/Twitter.
Kekova is a small, uninhabited island located in the Mediterranean Sea, in western Turkey.
Three stone anchors and some 30 amphorae were uncovered, according to the BBC.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition, told the BBC. "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."
Amphorae found during the excavations date back to the Bronze Age, approximately 4,400 to 4,700 years ago, shedding light on ancient maritime trade along the coasts of Anatolia.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years,” Öniz told BBC. "We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
Analysis of the vessels shape indicate that they had likely been produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley, similar to others found in Egypt, Troy, and Crete.
One of the amphora is unique, noted Ersoy, and features nine distinct markings as well as two holes in its body.
Residue indicates possibility sailors made their own food
The vessel is thought to have been used as a cheese or butter churn, indicating that Bronze Age sailors might have made their own food during long voyages.
Some of the amphorae contained a glossy residue, the BBC reported, citing Macquarie University archaeologist Dr. Karin Sowada.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she told BBC. "It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins.”
"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge, they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."
“We continue to illuminate Anatolia's maritime history with new discoveries, preserving our underwater cultural heritage to pass it on to future generation,” Ersoy wrote on X. “I congratulate Assoc. Prof. Dr. Hakan Öniz, who holds the scientific responsibility of the excavations, and all our colleagues who contributed their efforts.”
